meta.notes: The owner's self-insert, now Lily Fern by her ruling of 2026-11-13 (lily_surname_20261113). Drums on one number, bass on another, never both; she sings the harmony; the piano is Adela's, then Juno's (lily_instruments_20261113). She works for a price, residents and the night man alike, always offscreen and never explicit (lily_occupation_20261113); appointments stay held until the economy charges the fare. Holds nothing in the main case, is on no record of 19 July, has no thread from 14 to 26 July, and never learns who rides the night man: a good ear is not recognition. Her five cases (lf1_ to lf5_, design/ORISON_LILY_INVESTIGATOR_2026-11-13.md) are outside the solve chain; case 5 runs beside Stacy's and stands on Stacy's card. She calls the companion the Vantry. The earlier threads still exist to show Adela.

li_c1.line: Count her in and find out. I can bang things with a stick. She writes my entrance big enough to read in a coal hole, then moves it while I am still obeying.

li_c2.line: Because of the finish on the second one. When we both mean it, you can't get a glass filled in this room for a full minute. Some nights we look at each other and drop it and just laugh. That's good too. Mind the stand.

li_a1.line: I said yes in March, once somebody asked me. It's a good offer. She's sent it back with corrections, they've sent it back with fewer pages, and one of these days they get bored.

choices.label: She wants her name on it.

li_a2.line: She's right about the name. She's right about the picture. She'll be right about clause six until they stop writing. I want to hear what we sound like from outside. Once. Nobody in this room has ever heard that.

li_a3.line: Every Tuesday. She says "from the bridge."

li_f1.line: Don't. I've had the faces. Do you want a drink, or do you want to carry this? Juno Kells says she can play piano. She can't. We find out how much on Thursday.

li_f2.line: Other end. It's a bass fiddle, not a patient.

li_r1.line: They wrote. To the bar, she never gave them the shop. It came the Tuesday after. "We note your amendments. Clause six stands. Kindly advise." Nobody in Astoria reads the Record. I've got all seven of theirs in the bench, under the music, with her pencil on every one, and no correction twice.

li_r2.line: It's a test of an act. I wrote back: Miss Voss is dead, send the picture. Took me a week. It's the shortest thing they've had from this address.

li_r3.line: Don't you start. Everybody's got hold of what she wanted. She wanted eleven changes and a hat.

li_v1.line: It does. She took out her two bars at the end of June. I'd told her in March. Then you stood by the coat hooks and told her which bar, and she played it like scripture. Don't look at me, I was there. You had your coat on.

li_v2.line: Nobody remembers their good ones. You've got ears, for a man with a wrench. It went where it goes, two Saturdays out of three. I'm not sorry about that.

li_p1.line: Friday. Somebody over there has written on it in pencil. "Suggest smaller hat." It's the ugly one, I've got both arms and she's laughing at something off the edge. It's the only one of the two of us there is.

li_p2.line: Emil Voss has a wall. I'll take it round. I said I'll take it round.

li_p3.line: That's what I've been telling myself. You'd think it would sound better from a stranger.

li_d1.line: She told you too? She can't hold it, she's like a boiler. That's my bass on there. I'd like that reel more than anyone living.

li_d2.line: Miss Sato said no in May. All that's changed since is who's missing from the room. I've got a bench full of grease pencil. I'm not asking.

li_t1.line: Eleven people, one fight, and a man who wants the same waltz he wanted last week. I got paid in rice crackers. I'm told that's a raise.

li_n1.line: After the set. Juno's got a left hand now. I don't know where she got it. Nobody's listening, they've all got one eye on the door. I'm calling it a rehearsal. It's the most fun I've had since spring.

li_m1.line: Thursday. I was telling Juno about a B flat. I've never been so badly received in my life. She always wanted to know what the light was like. Nobody could tell her. Nobody looks at the light. I looked.

li_m2.line: It's on its way somewhere else. Mind, it pours away from you. Do you know anyone else with one of these? I want eleven. I'm asking everybody who's been asked.

li_m3.line: On the left. I know it's on the left. It was fine for eight bars. I put her two back, and in the ninth the left pin let go. Five weeks I went up and looked at nothing. It comes in slow. You want the light from the side. She'd have told me that.

li_m4.line: You've got eyes, for a man with a wrench. I've still got the tracing, on glass. I could go back. I've done the sums. I'm not going to.

li_m5.line: She'd want it eleven ways and a hat, and she'd want it to be my fault. It is my fault. Don't look at me, look at it, everybody else is.

li_m6.line: Tuesday. To the bar. "We note your client's billing. Under clause six, the Company retains the negative. Suggest smaller letters. Kindly advise." That's eight in the bench. I haven't got anyone to correct them.

li_w1.line: I've been up on roofs. Nothing's the matter. It's a very good moon. There isn't a mark on it. There's a professor in the Record on about smudges. I've told myself that's the plate.

lfa_r1.line: Working is a strong word for it lately. But yes. Two dollars the hour, paid before the curtain, and I keep the clock. You may have conversation, company, or the other thing, and you may change your mind at any point and keep your manners.

lfa_r2.line: She counts it, twice, then draws the curtain. The hour goes at her pace. Afterwards she ties her robe and asks what you were really hoping for, and doesn't wait for an answer.

lfa_r3.line: Then I'll play you something for nothing, which is worth about the same and costs me less.

lfa_r1b.line: I've been keeping fewer hours since July. The ones I keep, I keep properly. Two dollars, before the curtain. Same rules as ever.

lfa_r2b.line: She counts it, twice, then draws the curtain. The hour goes at her pace. Afterwards she ties her robe and asks what you were really hoping for, and doesn't wait for an answer.

lfa_r3b.line: Then I'll play you something for nothing, which is worth about the same and costs me less.

lfa_b1.line: Appointments. Initials, never names. A gentleman's wife once read it and found nothing but the weather, because I write the weather beside every one. You'd be surprised what a gentleman will confess while insisting he's never done anything wrong.

lfa_b2.line: What someone is lonely about, never. What someone means to do to somebody else, that's a different ledger. I keep that one in my head.

lf1_a1.line: Minnie. Rooms at Mrs. Hackett's on Thirty-first Street, or did. Mrs. Hackett says she left on the fourth, paid up, no forwarding. Her trunk went to the church sale. Her name's gone out of the register like it was never ink. And I have a note from her, in her hand, asking me to come.

lf1_a2.line: The sixth. Two days after Mrs. Hackett says she'd gone. Either Minnie wrote me from somewhere she can't say, or someone is very confident about the fourth.

lf1_a3.line: Women do. Not without their good shoes. She left her good shoes. Anyway, the note's dated the sixth, and Mrs. Hackett says the fourth.

lf1_b1.line: Two of her lodgers will talk to me who'd never talk to a policeman. One swears Minnie went out on the fourth with a man in a camel coat. The other swears she heard Minnie crying through the wall on the fifth. They don't agree, and they both think I'm unwell for asking.

lf1_b2.line: Scraped out on the fourth and written back in, in another hand, on a day the house says she was gone. And, darling, the page above has a lodger Stacy would know: a woman in a grey hat, one night in October. Small city. Ask her.

lf1_c1.line: He holds Minnie's debts. Bought them, from three shops and a doctor, and he collects in person. Minnie isn't missing. She's hiding. I could put his name in front of the right paper tomorrow. It would also tell him exactly which friends of hers to watch.

lf1_c2.line: Yes. I was always going to say that; I wanted to hear you say it too. We'll take his paper apart quietly: the debts, the doctor, the dates. Nobody needs her address for that.

lf1_c3.line: No. Not while she's on the run from him. I'll do it the slow way and you can be cross with me later. We take his paper apart quietly.

lf1_d1.line: The doctor's bill was written after the doctor died, which was clumsy of somebody. Two shops took theirs back. He can't collect on paper that's lying. Minnie sent word through a girl at the ferry: she's well and she's not coming back.

lf1_d2.line: One of them heard her cry through a wall she'd already left. I've decided to believe both lodgers. Funny how a respectable man can lose a fortune and remain respectable. A woman loses her room and suddenly nobody remembers she existed.

lf2_a1.line: Five notes. I heard them on Adela's piano last night with the lid down and nobody on the bench. Before you say it, Stacy already said it.

lf2_a2.line: Stacy, I think the piano remembers tomorrow.

lf2_a4.line: That is a separate and considerably less interesting problem. I've written the five notes down. There's sheet music in the bench with them on it, and it isn't Adela's hand or mine.

lf2_b1.line: A song-plugger's copy. Somebody sat in the back three Tuesdays running and wrote our arrangement out for a publisher on Twenty-eighth Street. And there's a tuner's boy across the light well who practises at night on a shop upright. Sound comes through that wall like it pays rent.

choices.label: So it was him you heard.

lf2_b2.line: Mostly. He learned our tune from the plugger's copy and plays it badly at one in the morning. That's the piano with the lid down, and the paper in the bench. Adela wants the copy back, with interest.

lf2_c1.line: The publisher sent a cheque and an apology, in that order, which is the right order. The tuner's boy plays something else now. It's worse. I like him.

lf2_c2.line: Nearly. Old Mr. Haskell at the end of the bar says I played those five notes at Christmas. I wrote them in March. He's never wrong about a tune. I'm not saying what that means. I'm saying I've stopped playing them.

lf3_a1.line: Mr. Truesdale. The one Stacy's exchange business nearly drowned in March; he swam. He's offered me fifty dollars to say he spent the night of the second of May with me, start to finish.

choices.label: Fifty dollars is a lot of rent.

lf3_a2.line: It is, and I'd like it, and that's exactly why I'm telling you instead of buying a coat. You can purchase my company, darling. My conscience is a separate establishment.

lf3_a3.line: A mail clerk at the exchange had her desk ledger burned that night, the one that would have put him in front of a judge. I'm going to pretend to think about his fifty dollars.

lf3_b1.line: I let him think so. He talks when he thinks he's bought something. He has the clerk's brother on his payroll, and the brother has four children. If I go to the police, Truesdale loses a ledger and the brother loses a living. I don't want to be the reason four children eat less.

choices.label: Then what were you doing on the second?

lf3_b2.line: Holding a dish of developer in Adela's darkroom till two in the morning, being told off for breathing. She writes every batch on a slip with the date and the time. If I'm going to refuse him, I'd like it on paper first.

lf3_c1.line: Second of May, ten to two, two batches, my initials where she made me sign for the spilt hypo. I wasn't with him. I can't be his alibi and I won't be. Now: do I send the slip to the clerk's lawyer, or keep it and tell Truesdale no to his face?

choices.label: Send it. Don't stand in front of him.
Tell him yourself. With Stacy there.

lf3_c2.line: Sensible. Stacy will say you put me up to it. I'll let her.

lf3_c3.line: He'll hate that. He'll hate it in front of a witness who pours his drinks. Good.

lf3_d1.line: No alibi, no fifty dollars, a lawyer with a slip in her file. The clerk keeps her job, and so does her brother, because I asked her lawyer nicely to leave him out of it.

lf3_d2.line: Still at large, as they say, and still very well dressed. Somebody pays for that stationery. I'd love to know who. I'm told that's how women like me end up in rivers.

lf4_a1.line: In my comic's mask, darling. A tall woman in black silk and a little domino going in and out of Steinway Street hotels, telling the night clerks she's Lilith. And telling one of them she's me, which is how a gentleman came to accuse me of taking his wallet in a room I've never seen.

lf4_a2.line: Someone who reads the strip. That narrows it to everybody who can read. Adela's portraits will tell us whose shoulders are whose.

lf4_a3.line: It was, until the wallet. I spent years becoming myself. If someone intends to impersonate me, I insist on better workmanship.

lf4_b1.line: Stacy sat the night clerks down one at a time. Three describe a woman my height. Two describe a man in a long coat and a lot of powder. One describes me, exactly, on the night of the ninth, when I was on this stage in front of fifty people playing the bass badly.

lf4_b2.line: Or he is. The rest is a pickpocket from Corona in borrowed silk who worked out that a hotel clerk looks at a mask and not at a man. Stacy has his name. I have my wallet back, figuratively.

lf4_c1.line: No. A pickpocket from Corona wore her clothes for three weeks. That's not the same thing at all, and I'll thank you not to say it in front of the strip.

choices.label: And the clerk who saw you on the ninth?

lf4_c2.line: He's sure. I was here. I don't need to be the more real one; I only need the wallet to be his and the night to be mine. He can keep the rest of it.

lf5_a1.line: Nobody sits there. I play to it. Stacy hasn't asked me to stop, which is how I know she wants to. We had a song half done. I'm going to finish it if it kills me, which is the kind of thing you shouldn't say in this bar any more.

lf5_a2.line: It doesn't have words yet. She used to say a song finds its words when it knows what it's for. I can remember every ridiculous thing she ever said to me. I can't remember whether I told her I loved her that morning.

lf5_a3.line: I sleep. I just do it at the piano. Fine. Tomorrow I'll show you something.

lf5_b1.line: The Ravenswood portrait. Her and my elbow. Look behind us, in the doorway: a man in a soft hat, looking at her, not at the camera. I think he's the one. I think I should have seen him.

lf5_b2.line: I found him. It took me nine days and I was rude to two people I love. He's the Ravenswood's bookkeeper. He was looking at her because she owed for the hall. That's all he is. I wanted him to be the answer so badly I made him one.

lf5_c1.line: Stacy says a great many things, all of them true and none of them helpful. She says loving Adela can't mean I put myself in the river after her. I say stopping is leaving her.

lf5_c2.line: I know. That's the unbearable part. She's found something, she says. A card in Adela's own pencil. Real, and dull, and true. I'm going to go and look at it like a grown woman.

lf5_d1.line: Stacy's card asks a question, and it's a real one, and it's on your wall where it belongs. The song had been waiting for that. Not for an answer. For something true to stand on.

lf5_d2.line: Tonight, after closing, for one listener and an empty chair. She made me feel like I was something worth remembering. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with that now. Play, I suppose.
